inline_text:
Following up on [my review of #9](https://github.com/aaif/wg-security-and-privacy/pull/9#discussion_r4073994177), as requested after the guide merged.

In [Section 2 at e757d35](https://github.com/aaif/wg-security-and-privacy/blob/e757d350133fea0858dda1deec13dbca923b3cf8/deliverables/DRAFT-agentic-ai-security-best-practices-guide.md#L30-L37), the confidential-computing row makes credential exposure “Not applicable (hardware-protected).”

Hardware isolation protects guest memory against host access within the platform's threat model. A bearer token released to guest software still grants its holder access. If that software exposes the token, its permissions and remaining validity determine the exposure. [RFC 6750 §1.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6750.html#section-1.2) defines this bearer property; [Intel's guest threat model](https://intel.github.io/ccc-linux-guest-hardening-docs/security-spec.html#threat-model) includes the guest software stack in the trusted computing base.

Proposed replacement cells:

- **Maximum Exposure Window:** Credential validity, subject to effective revocation; hardware isolation does not shorten token lifetime.
- **Blast Radius Scope:** Credential permissions if exposed by guest software. Hardware isolation protects against host access within the platform's threat model.

Add one sentence below the table: “Use confidential computing alongside short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials and controls on which guest components can access or release them.”

One correction to my original review: Azure REPORT_DATA binds a hash of runtime claims, including the vTPM key, VM configuration and user data. My earlier wording implied it could bind only the vTPM key. [Azure's design documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/confidential-computing/guest-attestation-confidential-virtual-machines-design#report-payload) describes the actual binding.

Done when the two cells and explanatory sentence are updated, with the bearer-token and platform-threat-model references.
